```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5,
  out.width = "90%"
)

library(ggplot2)
data("airquality")

# Remove rows with missing values for plots that need complete observations.
aq <- na.omit(airquality)

# Treat month as a category so ggplot2 displays separate groups.
aq$Month <- factor(
  aq$Month,
  levels = 5:9,
  labels = c("May", "June", "July", "August", "September")
)
```

# Introduction

This assignment demonstrates thirteen `ggplot2` geometries using R's built-in
`airquality` dataset. Each geometry creates a different type of visualization
or adds a visual element to a plot.

The `airquality` dataset contains daily air-quality measurements in New York
from May to September 1973.


## Inspect the data

```{r inspect-data}
head(airquality)
```

```{r data-structure}
str(airquality)
```

## Check missing values

```{r missing-values}
colSums(is.na(airquality))
```

Some observations contain missing values. For the examples below, `aq` is a
complete-case version of the dataset, created with `na.omit()`.

```{r cleaned-data}
dim(aq)
summary(aq)
```

# Visualizations using ggplot2 geometries

## 1. `geom_bar()` — Bar chart

`geom_bar()` counts the number of observations in each category by default.
Here, it shows how many daily records are available for each month.

```{r geom-bar, fig.cap="Number of observations in each month."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Observations per Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Number of observations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Each bar represents the number of complete daily records
for that month.

## 2. `geom_boxplot()` — Boxplot

`geom_boxplot()` summarizes the distribution of a numerical variable using
the median, quartiles, whiskers, and potential outliers.

```{r geom-boxplot, fig.cap="Distribution of ozone measurements by month."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Month, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange", alpha = 0.75) +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone Distribution by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Compare the median ozone level, spread, and potential
outliers across the months.

## 3. `geom_density()` — Density plot

`geom_density()` estimates and displays the distribution of a continuous
numerical variable as a smooth curve.

```{r geom-density, fig.cap="Estimated density distribution of ozone measurements."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Ozone)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightblue", color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Density Distribution of Ozone",
    x = "Ozone concentration",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Higher parts of the curve indicate ozone values where
observations are more concentrated.

## 4. `geom_histogram()` — Histogram

`geom_histogram()` divides a numerical variable into intervals (bins) and
displays the number of observations in each interval.

```{r geom-histogram, fig.cap="Frequency distribution of ozone measurements."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Ozone)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 15,
    fill = "skyblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Histogram of Ozone Levels",
    x = "Ozone concentration",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** The bars show how frequently ozone measurements fall
within each interval. Changing `bins` changes the number of intervals.

## 5. `geom_hline()` — Horizontal reference line

`geom_hline()` adds a horizontal line at a specified y-value. In this example,
the line marks the mean ozone concentration.

```{r geom-hline, fig.cap="Ozone and temperature with a horizontal mean reference line."}
mean_ozone <- mean(aq$Ozone)

ggplot(aq, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean_ozone,
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone and Temperature",
    subtitle = paste("Horizontal line = mean ozone:", round(mean_ozone, 1)),
    x = "Temperature (F)",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Points above the line have ozone values greater than the
dataset's mean; points below it have values lower than the mean.

## 6. `geom_jitter()` — Jitter plot

`geom_jitter()` adds a small amount of random displacement to points. This
helps reveal observations that would otherwise overlap.

```{r geom-jitter, fig.cap="Ozone measurements by month with jitter to reduce overlap."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Month, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_jitter(
    color = "blue",
    width = 0.18,
    height = 0,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone Measurements by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** The horizontal jitter separates points visually. It does
not change the original ozone measurements.

## 7. `geom_line()` — Line graph

`geom_line()` connects observations in x-axis order. Here, each month is
displayed as a separate series of daily temperatures.

```{r geom-line, fig.cap="Daily temperature observations, grouped by month."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Day, y = Temp, color = Month, group = Month)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Temperature by Month",
    x = "Day of month",
    y = "Temperature (F)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Each coloured line represents one month. The plot allows
us to compare daily temperature patterns, although the same day number in
different months does not represent the same date.

## 8. `geom_point()` — Scatter plot

`geom_point()` displays each observation as a point. It is commonly used to
explore the relationship between two numerical variables.

```{r geom-point, fig.cap="Relationship between temperature and ozone."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Temperature and Ozone",
    x = "Temperature (F)",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Look for an overall pattern in the points. An upward
pattern may suggest that higher temperatures are associated with higher
ozone measurements; a scatter plot alone does not establish causation.

## 9. `geom_rug()` — Rug plot

`geom_rug()` adds small marks along the plot axes to show the locations of
individual observations.

```{r geom-rug, fig.cap="Scatter plot with rug marks along both axes."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_rug(color = "red", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature and Ozone with Rug Marks",
    x = "Temperature (F)",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** The marks along the bottom and left edges show where
observations occur on the temperature and ozone scales.

## 10. `geom_smooth()` — Smoothed trend

`geom_smooth()` adds an estimated trend line. The `loess` method is useful for
showing a potentially nonlinear pattern in this dataset.

```{r geom-smooth, fig.cap="Smoothed relationship between temperature and ozone."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    color = "red",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature and Ozone Trend",
    x = "Temperature (F)",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** The curve summarizes the estimated relationship. The
shaded area is the confidence band around the fitted smooth.

## 11. `geom_text()` — Text labels

`geom_text()` places text at specified coordinates. This example adds an
annotation to the scatter plot.

```{r geom-text, fig.cap="Scatter plot with a text annotation."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 100,
    y = 100,
    label = "High ozone area",
    color = "red",
    size = 4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone Measurements with Text Annotation",
    x = "Temperature (F)",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** The annotation adds explanatory text at the chosen
coordinates. Its position is illustrative and is not itself a data point.

## 12. `geom_violin()` — Violin plot

`geom_violin()` displays the distribution of a numerical variable across
categories. The width of the violin represents the estimated data density.

```{r geom-violin, fig.cap="Distribution of ozone measurements across months."}
ggplot(aq, aes(x = Month, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "mediumpurple", alpha = 0.65, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone Distribution Across Months",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Wider sections indicate ozone values with a higher
estimated concentration of observations. Compare the shapes across months.

## 13. `geom_vline()` — Vertical reference line

`geom_vline()` adds a vertical line at a specified x-value. Here, the line
marks the mean temperature.

```{r geom-vline, fig.cap="Ozone and temperature with a vertical mean reference line."}
mean_temp <- mean(aq$Temp)

ggplot(aq, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean_temp,
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone and Temperature",
    subtitle = paste("Vertical line = mean temperature:", round(mean_temp, 1), "F"),
    x = "Temperature (F)",
    y = "Ozone concentration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Observations to the left of the line have temperatures
below the mean; observations to the right have temperatures above the mean.
